Vectors: data as lists of numbers
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
A computer can only handle numbers. This section clarifies how to describe a thing from the real world by a list of numbers and which calculations with such lists are allowed.
The dot product
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
Two vectors with the same number of components give a single number if you multiply their components pairwise and add the products.
Norms: the size of a vector
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
How large is a vector? There are several correct answers to this question.
Distances and units
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices

Two examples are similar if their vectors lie close together. This section measures distances, shows that the result depends on the chosen units and presents a method that makes the features comparable.
Angles and similarity
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
Two vectors can point in similar directions even if they have different lengths. This section measures the angle between them.
Matrices and the data matrix
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
A dataset consists of many vectors with the same number of components. This section combines them into a single table of numbers, a matrix, and establishes how to write and calculate with matrices.
The matrix–vector product
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices

The same weighted sum is to be computed for all examples of a dataset. For this purpose, this section introduces the product of a matrix and a vector and shows the two ways to read it: row by row or column by column.
Linear maps
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
A matrix is not only a table but also a rule of calculation that turns one vector into another.
The matrix product
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
Two linear maps applied one after the other again give a linear map, and therefore a matrix.
Transpose, symmetry and the Gram matrix
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices

If you swap the rows and columns of a matrix, you get its transpose. With it, all dot products of a dataset can be collected in a single matrix: the similarities of all examples to one another and the relationships of all …
Identity matrix and inverse
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
Some linear maps can be undone, others cannot. This section introduces the matrix that changes nothing and the inverse matrix that reverses a map, and it clarifies when the inverse exists.
Systems of linear equations
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
So far the input x was given and the output Ax was sought. This section asks the reverse question: which input produces a given output?
Independence, basis and rank
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
Some vectors in a list bring nothing new, because they can be put together from the others.
The determinant
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices
A linear map deforms the grid of the plane, and in the process areas become larger or smaller.
Elementwise calculations and tensors
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 1: Vectors and Matrices

Some coordinate systems are especially convenient: their axes are perpendicular to one another, and the unit has the same length on every axis.
Projection onto a line
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 2: Projection, Eigenvalues and Decompositions
A point lies off a line. Which point of the line is closest to it?
The best approximate solution
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 2: Projection, Eigenvalues and Decompositions
A system of equations with more equations than unknowns usually has no solution. Instead, this section looks for the unknowns that satisfy the system as well as possible.
Projection onto a subspace

The previous section found the closest point of a column space.
Quadratic forms
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 2: Projection, Eigenvalues and Decompositions
After the linear functions, the quadratic ones are the simplest functions of several variables.
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 2: Projection, Eigenvalues and Decompositions
A matrix rotates and stretches most vectors at the same time. Some directions, however, it does not rotate: an arrow in such a direction only becomes longer, shorter or flipped over.
Diagonalization and the spectral theorem
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 2: Projection, Eigenvalues and Decompositions
If you describe a matrix in a basis of its eigenvectors, it becomes diagonal: each coordinate is only multiplied by its eigenvalue, and coupled calculations break down into separate ones.
Positive definite matrices
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 2: Projection, Eigenvalues and Decompositions

A quadratic form is a bowl if it is positive everywhere except at the origin. This section gives this property a name and presents tests for checking it: via the eigenvalues, via the pivots and via determinants.
The singular value decomposition
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 2: Projection, Eigenvalues and Decompositions
Eigenvectors exist only for square matrices, and they are perpendicular to each other only for symmetric ones.
Approximation by matrices of low rank
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 2: Projection, Eigenvalues and Decompositions
The singular value decomposition orders the building blocks of a matrix by their size. If you leave out the small ones, a matrix of lower rank remains that can be stored with far fewer numbers.
The pseudoinverse
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 2: Projection, Eigenvalues and Decompositions
In Chapter 1, only a square matrix with independent columns had an inverse.
The condition number
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 2: Projection, Eigenvalues and Decompositions
Measured data are never exact, and a computer rounds at every step. How much does the solution of a system of equations change when the right-hand side is slightly wrong?

The derivative
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule
The derivative measures how strongly a function of one variable responds to a small change in its input.
The chain rule
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule

Many functions arise by substituting one function into another. The chain rule says how the derivative of such a composition follows from the derivatives of the parts: the factors of the individual stages are multiplied.
Partial derivatives and the gradient
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule
If a number depends on many inputs, you can change each input a little on its own and hold the others fixed.
Directional derivative and steepest ascent
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule
The partial derivatives say how the function responds when you change one input alone. If you shift all inputs at once in one direction, the directional derivative measures the slope.
The Jacobian matrix
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule
Many calculation steps produce not one number but several: a matrix–vector product turns one vector into another.
The chain rule for several variables
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule
Calculations with many variables are chains of functions with many inputs and outputs. The chain rule carries over to them: the Jacobian matrices of the stages are multiplied.
Differentiating with respect to vectors and matrices
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule
Gradients of expressions such as aᵀx, xᵀAx or ‖y-Ax‖² are needed again and again. This section first fixes the shape of each derivative and then derives the most important formulas componentwise.
The Hessian matrix and the quadratic approximation
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule
The gradient describes the tilt of the terrain, but not its curvature. The Hessian matrix collects the second partial derivatives.
Computational graphs
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule
A computer evaluates long formulas step by step, and each step is a simple operation with a known derivative.
Automatic differentiation
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule
With the computational graph, derivatives can be computed mechanically, without rearranging formulas and exactly up to the rounding of the elementary operations.
Numerical differentiation and the gradient check
Mathematical Foundations · Chapter 3: Derivative, Gradient and Chain Rule
You can also estimate derivatives without a formula: you evaluate the function at two nearby points and form the difference quotient.
